items.title:
We have found stable singularity on 3D Euler! 
https://t.co/40miuTjMvl

Our starting point is a phys...
items.content:
We have found stable singularity on 3D Euler! 
https://t.co/40miuTjMvl

Our starting point is a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to come up with an approximate answer, and then to argue stability around that to complete the proof.

The challenge so far has been that PINNs have not been successful in discovering singularities on the current problem. A common failure mode is PINNs converging to a trivial solution. We take special care to nudge our PINN to interesting regions through a combination of constraints, and we believe this is a novel way of making PINNs work for such hard optimization problems.

We also carry out a detailed study of the transport field of our approximate profile, and show it has promising properties of local outgoing flow, essential for proving linear damping, which is an important ingredient of overall stability.

We believe that such physics-informed and physics-centric AI are critical ingredients across many areas of research involving physical systems, and  LLMs  lack such physical grounding. 

We have been working on this problem for much of this year, and we just saw the announcement by Tristan on Euler with forcing. In contrast, we consider without forcing and use a PINN formulation.  @Caltech
items.author: @AnimaAnandkumar
items.summary: Anima Anandkumar (Caltech) announces a major result: her team found a stable singularity solution to the 3D Euler equations using a physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a starting point, then rigorously proving stability around it. She describes a novel method to prevent PINNs from collapsing to trivial solutions by constraining them toward interesting regions, plus a detailed analysis of the transport field showing local outgoing flow essential for proving linear damping. She argues physics-centric AI is broadly valuable for physical systems research.

Technical depth is high, framing is substantive rather than promotional, and engagement is exceptional (~783k views, 2708 likes, 325 retweets). BREAKING: OpenAI says it has a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, a $1M math problem unresolved for roughly 90 years.

OpenAI said it was produced by about 10,000 coordinating AI agents over 88 hours on an unreleased model it calls "significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra."

OpenAI also addressed this morning's accusation from NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, who said the company pressured him over credit for a related result:

"We congratulate Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster on their remarkable mathematical work. We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem."

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI says an unreleased model solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Probl...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI says an unreleased model solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem in 88 hours.

• The result: an initially smooth fluid at rest, with a smooth external force and finite energy throughout, does develop a singularity in finite time. The solution is a vortex spiraling inward and elongating like spaghetti
• OpenAI has been training the internal model since August 28, less than two weeks, and calls it significantly more capable than Astra. Training is still ongoing
• On September 1 they heard rumors two Millennium problems had been resolved elsewhere, and turned the model loose on all of them using coordinating agent swarms
• Roughly 10,000 concurrent agents on Navier-Stokes, reaching the result 88 hours later. Euler fell first, about 100 agents over 50 hours
• 2.7 million messages and 130 billion output tokens on Navier-Stokes alone. Lean formalization took another 17 hours via Astra
• Noam Brown says it cost millions of dollars to run
• The Clay Institute still lists the problem as unsolved, and its criteria are based on the unforced equations while this result addresses the forced version

@theojaffee: "It took seven years to solve the last Millennium Prize problem. It took 88 hours to solve this one. 88 hours is like three and a half days. It's not even four days. Crazy."

items.title: I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted w...
items.content:
I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted with integrity and generosity throughout.

Initially we believed the other team had also solved the problem. We wanted to collaborate and do a joint release. 

When we learned that they had Euler but not Navier-Stokes, we offered to let them go first, to suggest that they should be the ones to get the prize, and optionally for Tristan to be the lead author on a rewrite of the OpenAI proof. We felt it was challenging to offer the same to Levent (an Anthropic employee), who was not willing to talk or coordinate with us anyway. We were open to other solutions.

We would have greatly preferred coordination. We did not rush to publish even though the other team wasn't communicating with us. The team threatened us with unfounded accusations of plagarism.

Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different. It is also worth noting that our latest model can solve many, many other math problems.

It is true that we tried this because there were rumors on the internet last week that Anthropic's models had solved a millennium problem and we were curious if ours could do it too.

items.content_html:
I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted with integrity and generosity throughout.

Initially we believed the other team had also solved the problem. We wanted to collaborate and do a joint release.

When we learned that they had Euler but not Navier-Stokes, we offered to let them go first, to suggest that they should be the ones to get the prize, and optionally for Tristan to be the lead author on a rewrite of the OpenAI proof. We felt it was challenging to offer the same to Levent (an Anthropic employee), who was not willing to talk or coordinate with us anyway. We were open to other solutions.

We would have greatly preferred coordination. We did not rush to publish even though the other team wasn't communicating with us. The team threatened us with unfounded accusations of plagarism.

Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different. It is also worth noting that our latest model can solve many, many other math problems.

It is true that we tried this because there were rumors on the internet last week that Anthropic's models had solved a millennium problem and we were curious if ours could do it too.

items.title: Sparse MLA only attends to the top-K tokens, so the rest of the KV need not live on the GPU. Hybrid ...
items.content:
Sparse MLA only attends to the top-K tokens, so the rest of the KV need not live on the GPU. Hybrid HiSparse in vLLM builds on that, and a request keeps decoding after its KV stops fitting in HBM.

It keeps KV on the GPU while there is room. Under pressure a request releases its coldest pages to host memory, keeps a small hot buffer of what the indexer asks for, and keeps decoding instead of being preempted.

📊 Demonstrated on GLM 5.3, one 8× H200 node, full 1M context. Same host memory, configured concurrency 32: KV offloading kept 5-6 requests running. Hybrid HiSparse kept 19-25.

🔹 Hot pages are ordinary KV blocks from the same pool (Hybrid Memory Allocator)
🔹 One fused kernel resolves resident, hot and missing rows, CUDA-graph capturable
🔹 Prefix caching, OffloadingConnector, P/D imports and MTP keep working

Built by @RedHat_AI and @PrimeIntellect with the vLLM community. Planned for v0.30; pinned commit, flags and calculator are in the post👇
🔗 https://t.co/6y7u5Hfc8c

items.title: Synthetic data derived from production user data of consumer AI tools is used for training. I’ve hea...
items.content:
Synthetic data derived from production user data of consumer AI tools is used for training. I’ve heard this rumour from both large labs’ employees. 

In particular, if you’re doing something “interesting” like working on complex math/business/software/bio problems you’re dramatically more likely to get trained on because they filter/up-weight towards those usecases where the model has the most to learn.

Even in ZDR and “we won’t train on you” regimes, derivative data is usually carved out. The promise is only not to train on exactly the data you put in, rewritten data is fair game.

items.title: @ravinsharma7 well obviously the data gets 'touched'.. it's being processed by the provider. then th...
items.content:
@ravinsharma7 well obviously the data gets 'touched'.. it's being processed by the provider. then the question is do you store it or delete it once you're done processing, ZDR says you delete it.

what you choose define as "processing" a request is important, it will of course include generation of the response sent back to the user, but also a suite of other derivative actions like collection of analytics (stuff like using a model to classifying the usecase, safety screening, etc), billing data, and potentially synthetic data.

what you have to delete is the original request, derivate data you use to bill the customer, monitor use, keep product analytics, etc. are all almost always kept. It's not a huge leap to imagine that synthetic data could be considered to be derivative data.

Anyway, I have no specific knowledge beyond rumours I've heard but in a world with LLMs can observe, process, and manipulate data very very quickly, ZDR is a much weaker guarantee than you might think.
items.author: @aidangomez

He argues ZDR is a much weaker guarantee than commonly assumed in a world where LLMs can quickly process and manipulate data, while caveatting his claims as based on rumors rather than specific knowledge.

items.title: This new bill banning superintelligence could hobble the frontier AI industry (which aspires to buil...
items.content:
This new bill banning superintelligence could hobble the frontier AI industry (which aspires to build superintelligence even if it doesn’t actually know how to do so).

And the leaders of that industry have only themselves to blame.

There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not. It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive.

So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lacking of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten where we are, with intense mistrust all around.

Although I don’t think this bill is formulated correctly – and risks throwing out some beneficial applications along with some bad ones – I can see why legislators have reached this point.

By not playing straight, the big tech companies have soiled their own bed.

• Huawei is playin...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Huawei is orchestrating China's push to build its own ASML.

• Huawei is playing project management, investing across the supply chain and helping secure deals with fabs like SMIC
• A Bernstein analyst: a prototype achieves nothing on its own. You need thousands of vendors and customers moving together, and a central orchestrating power to bring the effort together
• Shanghai's Yuliangsheng co-developed the first Chinese-made advanced DUV machine and targets 12 units by the end of this year
• SMIC is testing it, and so is Huawei on its own production lines
• The bottlenecks are projection lenses and light sources. Yuliangsheng currently uses Zeiss lenses, and Zeiss says it only sells to ASML, so they came through the secondary market
• UBS puts Chinese lithography at roughly where ASML stood in 2004
• CXMT and YMTC have stockpiled enough ASML machines to cover three years of expansion

@theojaffee: "Zeiss said it only sold its optics to ASML. So how did they end up in China? It's possible to secure the lenses on the secondary market, whatever that means. The black market for smuggling precision optics."

Manually reading code is n...
items.content:
I haven't read a single line of AI-generated code in a couple of months.

Manually reading code is no longer effective for me.

Code is a low-bandwidth information source. The more you have, the harder it becomes to separate the signal from the noise.

Instead, I spend most of my time designing processes to automatically verify the code, write unit tests, evaluate the system while it runs, handle potential errors, and log and trace everything that happens.

Here is what the ideal cycle looks like:

Plan → Code → Deploy → Test → Monitor → Learn

The goal is to run this cycle automatically, end to end. The interesting part of this comes in the final three steps:

1. Test: We stress-test the running system by generating fake traffic or diverting some of the live traffic to it.

2. Monitor: Observability is always baked in as part of our coding practices, so here we monitor what happens with the system as much as we can.

3. Learn: We scan the telemetry data from the monitoring process and feed any errors into the plan for the next iteration to fix those issues.

@Dynatrace is one way to implement this pattern. You can use it to connect your agents and retrieve runtime information to feed into the planning process.

Basically:

• It will give you the telemetry data you need
• It will let your agents retrieve the runtime signals

For automated agents, you can run this feedback loop as a hook. Every change then passes through deployment, testing, observation, and analysis before completion.

Here is an explanation of the complete workflow:

https://t.co/QIQr20jYKA

Thanks to the Dynatrace team for partnering with me on this post.

items.title: Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr reveals why the term "AGI" is becoming useless just as we...
items.content:
Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr reveals why the term "AGI" is becoming useless just as we're getting closer to it:

"AGI as a term is kind of a fuzzy cloud. When it was a fuzzy cloud that was far away, you could say oh AGI and gesture towards it, and that was a useful thing to say. But we're now inside the fuzzy cloud of different things you might mean by AGI. It's not really very helpful to say is this AGI or is it not. It all depends on how you define it."

"It doesn't feel useful to talk about in the abstract is Astra AGI or not. People are trying to get at some tipping point. But people mean quite different tipping points."

"Are you talking about AI that can tip you into fully automated AI R&D, recursive self-improvement, intelligence explosion? Or AI that is a drop-in remote worker and can wipe out large chunks of the workforce. That's a different tipping point."

"An approach to jargon I keep coming back to is, if you can just say a short phrase instead of some jargon term, that's almost always better. If you can say super duper powerful AI, no really super powerful. Or if you mean AI that can kick off RSI, say that. The fact we have to have a whole discourse cycle about it shows this term is not very helpful."
@CSETGeorgetown

🔶 KV cache management matters. A packed KV layout for DeepSeek V4 saves ~10% KV memory and cuts 92 tensors per block down to 1
🔶 Parallelism follows the model. Decode context parallelism gives Kimi K3 2.7x decode throughput at the same TPOT; prefill context parallelism runs DeepSeek V4's sparse MLA 2.65x faster than head sharding
🔶 Simple scheduling makes an impact. Simply capping prefill breaks head-of-line blocking and achieves +93% TPGS and ~2.3x better p90 interactivity

4/6

items.content:
Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr explains why AI-enabled bio attacks could become a rare point of common ground between America and China:

"The right counterargument from a US perspective would be, okay, but maybe Chinese models will lead to bio attacks outside China that then affect China. Even if you have perfect censorship and perfect surveillance of all your citizens, maybe you can't stop someone outside China from doing this."

"Another one I've been thinking about is incident reporting after Hugging Face. There's a lot of questions around what happened here, and what conclusions we should draw."

"That's the kind of thing where I think it's very unlikely we'll get a handshake deal of we'll do X if you do Y, just because the trust isn't there."

"It needs to be something more like, hey, we think it would be a good idea if both of us do X, and we can just do it. It's cost-free for the US to say, look, we can start sharing some incidents with you. Trying to get them to come along, rather than trying to get some kind of hard commitment."
@CSETGeorgetown

items.title: Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr argues China may not actually want to race America to AGI...
items.content:
Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr argues China may not actually want to race America to AGI:

"It's really not clear to me that they are. They think of themselves as in competition with the US on AI. They wanna be leading the world of AI. There's a specific version of racing to recursive self-improvement so that you're the first one to get to takeoff so that you have a decisive strategic advantage forever. I really don't think that is a prominent set of ideas in China."

"Some people are like, well, if they only understood how powerful AGI will be, then obviously they would have to race. Which I think is not right, given how much they care about being in control."

"The Chinese Communist Party, their whole deal is staying in control, keeping society stable. If they thought there was a serious risk that they would lose control of AI, then that would not feel appealing to them."

"It often feels like there's a real nihilism behind the, oh well, we could try and prevent them, but we can't because China. That just seems so defeatist, giving up so early in the story."
@CSETGeorgetown

items.title:
Lessons learned, the hard way:
🔷 Pipeline parallelism is great on cold, long prompts. On warm agent ...
items.content:
Lessons learned, the hard way:
🔷 Pipeline parallelism is great on cold, long prompts. On warm agent turns that add a few hundred tokens, the bubbles eat the gain.
🔷 Decode context parallelism won on Kimi K3 but only matched DEP on DeepSeek V4. Parallelism has to follow the model's attention stack.
🔷 Load balancing doesn’t always beat simple session-sticky routing: for workloads with short inter-turn delays, preserving a warm KV cache can matter more than balancing the queue.

5/6

Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr reveals why China sees AI companions as a threat to the Communist Party even when they never criticize it:

"In China, everything you do online is tied back to your SIM card, which is tied back to your national ID card. They can look at anything anyone is doing online and trace back to an individual person."

"There's one thing, does the AI tell you the Communist Party is bad. But there's a different thing, does AI cause social effects that have knock on dissatisfaction with the Communist Party. Their most recent regulation was actually on AI companions. They called it human-like AI. Read the f---ing regulation."

"The motivation there is less AI companions will tell their users that the CCP is bad, and more like if you have kids committing suicide, if you have these broader negative effects on society, is that bad for their hold on power. That's the primary lens they're looking at all this through."
@CSETGeorgetown

Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr explains what would actually count as a win in the upcoming Trump-Xi AI talks:

"We should start with low expectations. The really low expectations version would be nothing happens whatsoever. The low expectations version will be they'll both say in their readout something something artificial intelligence."

"Two years ago we had some engagement between China and the Biden White House, and there we got some joint language around managing the risks from AI and ensuring broad benefit. If we see similarly generic overarching language, that will also be a pretty low expectations version of the summit, which is pretty likely."

"If both sides name a more specific set of challenges that they're both interested in, not just maximizing benefits and minimizing risks, that'll be a win."

"If you figure out who should talk to who after this Trump-Xi meeting, that's kind of interesting progress as well."
@CSETGeorgetown

items.content:
Georgetown CSET Executive Director @hlntnr explains why China thinks it takes AI safety more seriously than America does:

"The problem is that both sides take it seriously in their own way. Sometimes in the US there's a sense that China is kind of a little bit behind us on this path to taking AI more seriously. But actually they sort of have the flip side, the same view of us."

"There was this really interesting piece that came out a week or two ago. The title was 'Anthropic Has American Disease.' It was criticizing the US government for not being serious on AI regulation."

"From the Chinese perspective, China has all these regulations, technical standards, all this stuff going on with their generative AI sector, and the US is really unserious because everything we're doing is voluntary."

"So both sides think that the other is not taking it seriously. For me it's less like will China be serious enough, and more like can they identify some specific concrete issue where they don't just talk past each other?"
@CSETGeorgetown

SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI released ChatGPT Images 2.5, and you can now draw instead of prompting.

• Sketch lets you draw directly in ChatGPT and show it what you have in mind, rather than writing a prompt
• Two variants, Flare for speed and Sunburst for quality
• Faster generation, improved fidelity, consistent details across multiple edits, and comment-based edits that change only what you specify
• C2PA metadata and invisible watermarking on everything it produces

@schisofrenia: "Every sort of AI-generated image, a few years later you can recognize subtle AI flavors that it has, tells that it was generated. This always becomes apparent, and then you're just gonna regret it later."

items.content_html:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI released ChatGPT Images 2.5, and you can now draw instead of prompting.

• Sketch lets you draw directly in ChatGPT and show it what you have in mind, rather than writing a prompt

• Two variants, Flare for speed and Sunburst for quality

• Faster generation, improved fidelity, consistent details across multiple edits, and comment-based edits that change only what you specify

• C2PA metadata and invisible watermarking on everything it produces

@schisofrenia: "Every sort of AI-generated image, a few years later you can recognize subtle AI flavors that it has, tells that it was generated. This always becomes apparent, and then you're just gonna regret it later."

items.title: HelixNano + Red Queen Bio CEO @hannu warns we're moving toward a world where someone could engineer ...
items.content:
HelixNano + Red Queen Bio CEO @hannu warns we're moving toward a world where someone could engineer a civilization-ending virus in a garage lab:

"Part of the founding thesis of the company was that open weight models will trail the frontier models but still end up being quite capable over time. It's going to be very hard to control those capabilities with any safeguards, so we have to assume that the capabilities are out there and widely diffused."

"As a general statement, it's not necessarily that we think it's possible right now for someone to have a garage lab and create a civilization-ending virus. But the second derivative of the capabilities is definitely pointing in the direction of that being possible sooner than we would like."

"There's other categories of actors, well-funded organizations or rogue states who are already being quite significantly uplifted."
@HelixNano

items.title:
We asked @TencentHunyuan authors why generating a harder coding task keeps failing.

They said a use...
items.content:
We asked @TencentHunyuan authors why generating a harder coding task keeps failing.

They said a useful terminal task has to keep four things consistent: the public instruction, the workspace, the official script, and the hidden tests.

One mismatch can invalidate the entire task.

> Script fails in the container
> Tests check a missing file
> Hidden rule the agent never sees

Their paper grows a verified child from a parent. Official scripts went from 67 lines to 374 (5.6x). The public instruction only went 85 words to 122 (1.4x).

A frozen DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 fell from 90% to 2.5% on later rounds. Yield still held around 500 accepted tasks per 1,000 attempts.

The extra work is real, and a longer README is the wrong knob.

> When would you auto-generate shell training tasks?
> If the official script passes, is that enough to train on?
> Which exam is the factory never allowed to rewrite?

Full Breakdown ↓↓

I used to work on computer vision models for robots and drones, and nothing is slower than having to run the robot in order to test your code.

This promises to solve that.

They will build a digital twin that will simulate the physical world.

Digital twins are virtual models of real physical objects or systems that use real-world data to reflect how the real physical object behaves. You can use these digital twins to test everything.

items.title:
AI Engineering is a lot more than learning how to prompt a model.

Yesterday, I told the story of a ...
items.content:
AI Engineering is a lot more than learning how to prompt a model.

Yesterday, I told the story of a developer who can't use AI at work and is afraid of falling behind, and many people replied, saying that it would take almost no time to learn everything required to become an effective AI Engineer.

I don't think that's the case.

Attached is a skill map for using coding agents. This image was published by @AndrewYNg last week.

We are well past the point where coding with AI is as simple as prompting a model. As we learn how to tame these tools, the work is becoming more and more nuanced, and we are developing patterns and techniques that require time to learn and master.

If you are a professional developer, you will be fine and adapt to the new ways, but it won't be easy. It won't take a week.

I found Andrew's article very good, so I'm linking to it below.

HelixNano + Red Queen Bio CEO @hannu predicts a future where everyone wears a device that detects new pathogens in their blood and synthesizes an mRNA countermeasure on the spot:

"On the design side, we actually definitely have a defender advantage. It's easier to break things than to design them. If someone wants to design a super virus, it's a much harder task than figuring out how to block that."

"On the deployment side right now, the attacker definitely has an advantage. They don't have to worry about regulation. They don't have to make a lot of virus to release it."

"Advertising my last book DARKOME, which has a scenario where we've had a ton of both engineered and natural pandemics in the next 20 years, and the end state is that everyone has an mRNA wearable."

"So everyone has a wearable device that can both sequence new pathogens from your bloodstream, and then in situ using microfluidic synthesis to make countermeasures right there."

"With enough effort, create a phase shift in the definitive defender advantage direction."
@HelixNano

items.title: HelixNano + Red Queen Bio CEO @hannu explains why we've had so few civilization-scale pandemics, and...
items.content:
HelixNano + Red Queen Bio CEO @hannu explains why we've had so few civilization-scale pandemics, and why engineered pathogens could break that pattern:

"In the natural zoonotic context, there's a number of things that have to align for the pandemic to be really bad. In the case of flu, you have to have certain mutations or recombination events that lead to a version of the virus that jumps from animals to humans."

"It's sufficiently distinct from previous infections we might have had that it spreads. There were possibly all kinds of pre-exposure to previous viruses that actually made Spanish flu worse, factors that we don't fully understand."

"In the case of COVID, we've had other coronaviruses circulating amongst humans before, including SARS and then milder ones. Origins of COVID shrouded in mystery. It is a narrow set of naturally occurring parameters that have to click together for something to become really bad and global."

"Through our global interconnectivity and air travel, the increased surface area between humans and nature, and climate shifting populations and migrations of animals, might make it more likely for there to be a higher frequency of natural pandemics."

"But I think overwhelmingly we are making it easier to engineer synthetic pathogens, that going forward is going to be the factor that dominates."
@HelixNano

items.title: HelixNano + Red Queen Bio CEO @hannu explains how we could pre-build defenses against future enginee...
items.content:
HelixNano + Red Queen Bio CEO @hannu explains how we could pre-build defenses against future engineered viruses before they even exist:

"One core assumption currently is that regardless of what level of threat an engineered pathogen ends up representing, right now the models can't really generate things that are fully out of distribution. We don't expect them to be able to create completely novel viruses."

"That means that any threat will likely be based on some scaffold from an existing viral family. If we can actually pre-build very broad countermeasures across those viral families, regardless of how dangerous the payload of the virus is, that should allow us to intervene across all of those scenarios."

"The same tools also let you go fast on the design side if something truly new appears and you don't have a pre-built countermeasure. But it is quite a strong move to just say, okay, we know that there's 11 plus families that are potential starting points. Let's see if we can cover them all."
@HelixNano

items.title:
I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.

As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we...
items.content:
I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.

As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we find more and more things to be productive about (and I don't want everything in my life to actually be productive), I have been testing and experimenting with AI usage in different contexts.

And Codex live voice mode opened up new options for me.

One time, instead of waiting to clean my apartment at the end of the day or on the weekend, I actually did it during the workday while I was dictating to Codex and processing tasks that I had to do.

Another time, I had to fill out this form for my Apple Business account. And Codex did it all for me - it even found my W-9 on my laptop to pull my EIN. It completed the whole form so that I could run errands.

Instead of being strapped to my computer and having to dig up all these files and numbers on my own, I could do double duty and get personal things off my plate without losing time.

I use AI on walks. And importantly, it's not that I'm adding AI to the walks that I'm already doing (for that, I still prefer Sam Cooke or Hello Puzzlers). It's that I'm able to TAKE MORE WALKS that I wasn't able to before because of AI.

So now, I might go on a walk at 4pm and process all the Slack messages that I didn't respond to or review a client contract. As a team, sometimes we even take team-wide walk breaks to work 1:1 with our AIs.

BUT. 

I just tried one new workflow that I hated with the fury of a thousand suns.

And that was trying voice mode while I was in the shower.

It was effective in the sense that the AI could hear me well and could process tasks (unlike the Apple AI assistant who shall remain nameless, who can't hear me if a single pin is dropped in the background).

Sure, there was a little annoyance when the phone had a permission pop-up and I had to reach my hand out of the shower to press it.

But my biggest gripe was that I just hated the overall experience. Hated it. 

There are some parts of my life that I really don't want to add AI into right now.

And it's really in those times where I allow my brain to dance off into the edges of my imagination, or truly relax and take time away from execution.

And I just want this to be a reminder that we need space to be away from tech and just think and exist.

That could be on a nature hike, or in the shower, or my favorite meditative place in the whole wide world (the middle of a car wash).

There is no perfect optimization formula that is telling us that every minute of every day has to be AI-enabled.

So I will no longer be showering with my AI and will stick to my rubber duck.

Thank you.

@milan_milanovic The way I think about this:

How do you evaluate both activities? What are the succ...
items.content:
@milan_milanovic The way I think about this:

How do you evaluate both activities? What are the success criteria?

In code generation, success is working software. In writing, success is connecting with the reader.

I think models do a good job at code generation right now (either aided by developers or alone in simple builds), but they don't do a good job at writing good prose.

So, unless this changes, people will keep pushing back on using AI for writing while they embrace it for code generation.

items.title: I never look at the code when I work on ChapterPal. I didn't do that even when Claude Code didn't ex...
items.content:
I never look at the code when I work on ChapterPal. I didn't do that even when Claude Code didn't exist yet and I copied and pasted the code from the chat into the text file.

But sometimes you have to. This usually happens when your code hits the limits of the cloud service for something so simple that isn't supposed to hit any limit, so you are curious and ask the bot the question: why did it hit this particular limit (e.g., memory or CPU time)?

If you want to understand the kind of code Codex writes, here's an example that I found today when I asked that question. So the task was: I needed to create a digest of a large book to send to an LLM and ask for an executive summary. I set the maximum size of the digest to be 100,000 characters.

The approach was to take all headings, the first and the last paragraphs of each first-level section of each chapter, the full content of the introduction and conclusion chapters, and, if 100,000 characters weren't reached yet, fill the remaining space with statistically important paragraphs of each chapter in proportion to the chapter's length.

So, why would Supabase crash the execution of such a simple algorithm, saying that all CPU available to the edge function was consumed?

The answer is: Codex implemented the algorithm as follows. To decide whether to append a statistically important paragraph to the digest, it needed to know what size the digest will have after the concatenation. How did it decide to implement this? The way no good software engineer would choose:

1. Loop over all paragraphs:

2. Concatenate the current digest with the candidate paragraph.

3. Measure the length of the resulting concatenation.

4. If more characters than 100,000, pick another paragraph and repeat.

What would a non-retarded software engineer do to get the resulting length? Add A+B, where A is the length of the current digest (computed once for the entire digest) and B is the length of the paragraph (computed once for each paragraph).

So, I sad to Codex to replace the length function with a + sign and this fixed the issue.

So, if you don't read the vibe code, it's almost entirely retarded like that. And that's OK. You should just be aware of the fact and not make it responsible for running a nuclear factory.

items.title: I am pleased to see that OpenAI’s new model is roughly on par with Gemini Flash and Opus 4.8 on prom...
items.content:
I am pleased to see that OpenAI’s new model is roughly on par with Gemini Flash and Opus 4.8 on prompt injection risk. Nice work!

Evaluating and naming other labs turns out to be a great way to encourage them to train more aligned models. We will continue to do this until other labs pay more attention to safety. This is good for everyone and there is a lot of room left to go!

We solved prompt injection in practice for Claude models about two months ago. But prompt injection is a significant security risk no matter what model you use, and it is important that the industry similarly spends more effort to train their models to be resistant to prompt injection, among other elements of model alignment.

As models become more capable and central to businesses and economies, the risks only increase. We should be taking them seriously, and doing the right thing for our customers and the world.

items.content:
Get "Mathematics of Machine Learning" here: https://t.co/07exFk6jgj by @TivadarDanka v/ @PacktDataML
—
GitHub: https://t.co/2ENjzhrAVa
—
Here is my review:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝘁 𝗢𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲

This massive book is incredible, with its comprehensive coverage of numerous fields of mathematics and their intersection with the world of AI, data science, and machine learning (AI+DSML). I remember the very first time that I encountered machine learning. This was 20+ years ago, and that was already after 20+ years of being drenched in advanced mathematics as an astrophysicist. 

That first encounter of mine with ML was this definition: "Machine learning is the set of mathematical algorithms that learn from experience" (slightly paraphrased from the original quote by Tom Mitchell, CMU). That definition surprised me, confused me, motivated me, and changed the course of my career from astrophysics into AI+DSML. 

This book by Tivadar Danka captures the full meaning of that definition. The book covers thoroughly the many areas and domains of mathematics through which patterns in data are detected, described, learned, and recognized - all for the benefit of powering ML and AI algorithms, applications, and aspirations. 

This book will motivate you, surprise you, and inspire you in many ways, no matter what level of mathematics has (or has not) already propelled your career journey. There is room for all of us to grow. 

This is a great book, worthy to sit on everyone's desktop, ready to help you explore and exploit the full set of mathematical algorithms that learn from experience. 

The book is accompanied by a rich GitHub code repository of Jupyter notebooks. Learn by doing! Do by learning!

Disclosure: the publisher provided me with a free review copy of the book.

items.title: December 2020. Years ago, I was already working through the mathematics and computational formulatio...
items.content:
December 2020. Years ago, I was already working through the mathematics and computational formulations surrounding George Gabriel Navier–Stokes: Poisson pressure equations, Burgers’ equations, momentum equations, discretization, CFD, and their implementation in #HPC. I explored these equations in my articles, written book, and research, not claiming the Millennium problem was solved, but trying to understand and computationally attack the mathematics behind the problem. Remarkable to see this same problem now at the center of frontier AI research.  Any claimed proof must still withstand independent mathematical scrutiny and ultimately satisfy the Clay Mathematics Institute’s acceptance process before the Millennium Prize problem can be regarded as formally resolved.

At the time, I wrote explicitly: “However, there still remains an unsolved aspect of the Navier-Stokes equation. The Clay Mathematics Institute has identified this as part of the top seven most significant open problems in mathematics and has offered a US$1 million prize for a solution or counterexample.” - GP

items.title: @llama_index hosted an executive suite at the US Open in NYC on Friday night and we shared the night...
items.content:
@llama_index hosted an executive suite at the US Open in NYC on Friday night and we shared the night session with AI Leaders building some of the most document-intensive AI apps 🎾 

Our team got to watch Venus and Serena play doubles together (surreal to see the sisters out there!), plus Ben Shelton vs Denis Shapovalov. 

Former USA top 50 player Mackenzie McDonald also stopped by our suite and spent time to chat with the team and everyone who came out. He said two things that map surprisingly well to building a company:

🐹 It's a hamster wheel. You have to keep proving yourself, and people forget what you did last time out. Doesn't matter how good the last result was.

😰 A lot of it is the mental game. Nobody sees the grit that goes into the smaller tournaments - he mentioned flying into a pretty remote part of China a few weeks ago for one.

Both of those hit close to home: you have to keep building and scaling faster, and staying relevant in a fast-changing landscape. Most of what we do here is not just what we put out on socials, but the massive amount of work nobody knows happened.

Thanks to @mackiemacster for coming by, and to everyone who joined us!

A bug surfaces

Fast code. Slow everything else.

items.title: @star33_0 Additional note: in my courses, occasionally a student came to me and said that they have ...
items.content:
@star33_0 Additional note: in my courses, occasionally a student came to me and said that they have the older edition, and they wanted to know if they need to buy another edition. I sometimes told them 'no' (**see below), but that they then needed to be more attentive to content that I presented in class that was not in the older version of the textbook. For mathematics courses, there is probably not such a huge addition of new content in the new edition, though the homework exercises and chapter examples & sample problems could be vastly different. 

** I taught data science and database courses primarily, which are disciplines where the industry skill requirements, applications, methods, and algorithms were evolving fairly quickly and substantially. So, I strongly recommended in the first day of class and in the syllabus that the students should not buy the older edition (if any) of the textbook.

items.content:
A new excellent textbook "Partial Differential Equations" by Victor Ivrii (2026) is now in @ChapterPal's collection.

The book provides material for learning partial differential equations through detailed coverage of wave equations, heat diffusion, and separation of variables techniques.

The textbook has many exercices in addition to those that ChapterPal can generate for the reader based on what they have read.

Here's the link: https://t.co/JHqLaM9chu

If an exercise is hard, ask ChapterPal for a hint. If still no luck, ask to explain how to approach this kind of exercises based on what you have read so far.

Reading on ChapterPal is like reading next to a patient tutor who is always there to unblock you and let you continue reading without feeling that you accepted to give up on a pice of knowledge in order to continue.

Below is the book's table of contents:

Chapter 0: Preliminaries
  - 0. Preface
  - 0.1. What one needs to know?
    * Multivariable Calculus
Chapter 1: Introduction

    * What is a PDE?
    * Where PDEs are coming from?
    * Examples of PDEs
    * Where are theorems?
  - 1.2. Initial and Boundary Value Problems

    * Notion of "well-posedness"
  - 1.3. Classification of equations
    * Linear and nonlinear equations
    * Elliptic, hyperbolic and parabolic equations

    * Diffusion equation
    * Laplace equation

Introduction to Modern Statistics (2nd edition) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin (2024) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of interactive books.

The book has 349 illustrations and 494 original interactive exercises (in addition to quizzes that ChapterPal can generate on demand based on the read content).

Read the textbook with an AI tutor: https://t.co/a8Kfpwp8tq

Here's the textbook's table of content:

Part I: Introduction to Data

Chapter 1: Hello data
  - Case study: Using stents to prevent strokes
  - Data basics
    * Observations, variables, and data matrices
    * Types of variables
    * Relationships between variables
    * Explanatory and response variables
    * Observational studies and experiments
  - Chapter review
    * Summary
    * Terms
  - Exercises
Chapter 2: Study design
  - Sampling principles and strategies
    * Populations and samples
    * Parameters and statistics
    * Anecdotal evidence
    * Sampling from a population
    * Four sampling methods
  - Experiments
    * Principles of experimental design
    * Reducing bias in human experiments
  - Observational studies
  - Chapter review
    * Summary
    * Terms
  - Exercises
Chapter 3: Applications: Data
  - Case study: Olympic 1500m
  - Simpson's paradox
  - Interactive R tutorials
  - R labs

Part II: Exploratory Data Analysis

Chapter 4: Exploring categorical data
  - Contingency tables and bar plots
  - Visualizing two categorical variables
    * Bar plots with two variables
    * Mosaic plots
  - Row and column proportions
  - Pie charts
  - Waffle charts
  - Comparing numerical data across groups
  - Chapter review
    * Summary
    * Terms
  - Exercises
Chapter 5: Exploring numerical data
  - Scatterplots for paired data
  - Dot plots and the mean
  - Histograms and shape
  - Variance and standard deviation
  - Box plots, quartiles, and the median
  - Robust statistics
  - Transforming data
  - Mapping data
  - Chapter review
    * Summary
    * Terms
  - Exercises
Chapter 6: Applications: Explore
  - Case study: Effective communication of exploratory results
    * Keep it simple
    * Use color to draw attention
    * Tell a story
    * Order matters
    * Make the labels as easy to read as possible
    * Pick a purpose
    * Select meaningful colors
  - Interactive R tutorials
  - R labs

Part III: Regression Modeling

Chapter 7: Linear regression with a single predictor
  - Fitting a line, residuals, and correlation
    * Fitting a line to data
    * Using linear regression to predict possum head lengths
    * Residuals
    * Describing linear relationships with correlation
  - Least squares regression
    * Gift aid for first-year at Elmhurst College

    * Extrapolation is treacherous
    * Describing the strength of a fit
    * Categorical predictors with two levels
  - Outliers in linear regression

  - Exercises
Chapter 8: Linear regression with multiple predictors

    * Summary
    * Terms
  - Exercises
Chapter 9: Logistic regression
  - Discrimination in hiring
  - Modelling the probability of an event
  - Logistic model with many variables
  - Groups of different sizes
  - Chapter review
    * Summary
    * Terms
  - Exercises
Chapter 10: Applications: Model
  - Case study: Houses for sale
    * Correlating with `price`
    * Modeling `price` with `area`
    * Modeling `price` with multiple variables
  - Interactive R tutorials
  - R labs

items.content:
Here are some of the coolest features of Hyper3D WorldGen:

• The model will automatically identify all of the objects in the scene and render them independently. You can edit, modify, or remove them.

• Every object will keep the spatial relationship and physics properties from the input image.

• You can control the camera, the composition, and the object placement of all of the assets in the scene.

• The world you generate is navigable and interactive, which is really fun to explore.

• You can export everything straight into Blender, Unity, and Unreal Engine for game dev, embodied AI, and virtual production pipelines.
